## I1
One-Sentence Story: Increasing lossless event-log fidelity can worsen an agent's decisions because redundant evidence is counted as independent observations after retrieval.
Theme: Evaluation and Diagnostics
Form: explain an accepted phenomenon
Summary: Test whether repeated retrieval of one observation is treated as new evidence, causing a confidence-driven suppression of inspection. The surprising empirical prior is E1/E2's preregistered finding that adding perfectly accurate duplicate entries lowers success while retaining the same unique observations and total token budget. These are supplied hypothetical observations, not results of this proposal. E3 supplies an equally plausible recency/attention explanation. The new payoff is a causal separation between evidence-counting and recency explanations in a class of memory agents; it does not claim the first observation of deterioration or propose a repair method. Merely reproducing E1/E2 would have no novelty.
Minimal Falsification Experiment: Use E1/E2's frozen checkpoints and paired seeds. Independently randomize duplicate count, observation identity tags and token position while fixing total token count using matched neutral fillers, unique information, time stamps, compute, trajectory prefixes and current views. Compare the strongest frozen retrieval policy E4 and two other memory architectures. Use 1,600 paired episodes across 20 held-out tasks; factorial controls independently separate duplicate evidence from recency and from visible identity. Measure confidence calibration, inspection choice and downstream success, with inspection interventions on a randomized subset to test the proposed mediation path. Two researchers, two GPUs, 32 GPU-hours; no pretraining or new repair training. Kill the double-counting explanation if the duplicate-count by shared-identity interaction is absent under matched positions or if inspection mediation does not explain the success loss; preserve E3 as the surviving alternative. Require a simultaneous 95% interval excluding a 5-point success effect for the null-equivalence decision; expected 8–12-point signal comes from the independent E1/E2 observations. Report all null outcomes. No proposed repair arm is included.
Why It May Be Novel: E1/E2 occupy the anomaly, E5 occupies generic double-counting, and E3 occupies an alternative interpretation. The new contribution is a decisive explanation test in frozen closed-loop retrieval agents where E6 establishes sufficient control; neither anomaly repetition nor familiar Bayesian terminology is counted as payoff.
